table.name: High Octane Ignition Timing Map (16x16)
table.description: Sets the high-octane timing adjustment for each engine-speed and cylinder-filling point. Values are degrees added to calculated base timing: +5 adds 5 degrees of advance, 0 adds nothing, and -5 removes 5 degrees. These are timing adjustments, not the final spark angle. Knock, idle and other corrections can change the final timing.

table.name: High Octane Ignition Timing Map Knock Window
table.description: Permits knock-control evaluation at each speed/load cell of the high octane timing schedule. 1 means evaluation is permitted; 0 means it is not permitted through this cell control. This is an on/off map, not a duration, crank-angle window or sensor sensitivity value. It shares storage with the timing map but edits only the permission bit, preserving the timing adjustment. It has not been established as a global disable of all knock functions.

table.name: High Detonation Ignition Timing Map (16x16)
table.description: Sets the alternate timing adjustment used by the detonation-protection schedule. Values are degrees added to calculated base timing: +5 adds 5 degrees of advance, 0 adds nothing, and -5 removes 5 degrees. Read each cell at its engine speed and cylinder filling. This schedule is separate from the amount of timing removed by the Knock Retard Limit maps; other corrections still affect final spark timing.

table.name: High Detonation Ignition Timing Map Knock Window
table.description: Permits knock-control evaluation at each speed/load cell of the high detonation timing schedule. 1 means evaluation is permitted; 0 means it is not permitted through this cell control. This is an on/off map, not a duration, crank-angle window or sensor sensitivity value. It shares storage with the timing map but edits only the permission bit, preserving the timing adjustment. It has not been established as a global disable of all knock functions.

table.name: Target AFR MBT Compensation Table
table.description: Adjusts the mixture-related factor in the MBT timing calculation. MBT means the timing calculated to produce best torque. Read the curve by target lambda: 1.0 is stoichiometric, below 1.0 is richer, and above 1.0 is leaner. Values are a percentage-form calculation factor, not degrees of advance or an AFR target. A larger factor does not necessarily mean more final ignition advance.

table.name: Crank Inj Atmospheric Pressure Compensation
table.description: Adjusts the fuel calculation while the engine is cranking, according to its atmospheric/environment input. The horizontal axis is an internal input index; it has not been converted to pressure in kPa. Values are displayed as a percentage-form compensation factor. Do not read the axis as altitude or the cells as an AFR target; a complete final-fuel change formula is not established here.

table.name: Injection End Timing Map 1
table.description: Schedules when an injection event ends, using engine speed and load. Values are angular timing values in degrees, not injector on-time in milliseconds. The angle reference and the complete conditions selecting this schedule are not explained by the current evidence, so an increase should not be described as earlier or later injection without that reference.

table.name: Injection End Timing Map 2
table.description: Alternate schedule for when an injection event ends, using engine speed and load. Values are angular timing values in degrees, not injector on-time in milliseconds. This is a separate schedule rather than an extra fuel multiplier. Its angle reference and complete selection conditions remain unresolved, so the direction of a timing change is not labelled earlier or later.

table.name: Startup ISC Airflow Engine Speed Compensation
table.description: Scales the extra idle-air quantity used during startup, according to engine speed. ISC means idle-speed control. This is a direct multiplier: 1.0 leaves this contribution unchanged, 1.2 makes it 20% larger, and 0.8 makes it 20% smaller. It works with Startup ISC Airflow Initial Value and Decay Value; it does not directly set idle RPM.

table.name: Fuel Injector Latency at 14V
table.description: Base injector opening delay at 14 volts, displayed in milliseconds. This accounts for time spent opening the injector before effective fuel delivery. Increasing the value adds more time compensation at the reference voltage; it does not change injector flow capacity. Voltage compensation and later fuel calculations also apply.

table.name: Fuel Injector Latency Adder
table.description: Voltage-related part of injector opening-delay compensation, displayed in milliseconds per volt. It works with Fuel Injector Latency at 14V rather than specifying an injector pulse by itself. A larger value means a larger voltage-related compensation term. Its effect at a particular voltage depends on the complete latency formula; do not treat it as milliseconds simply added at every voltage.

table.name: Transient ADV Addend Table A
table.description: An addition used by the transient ignition calculation as operating conditions change. The axis and cells remain internal ECU counts because their complete physical interpretation is unresolved. Increasing a cell increases the stored addition, but it cannot currently be translated into a stated number of degrees at the spark plug. ADV refers to advance; it is not a confirmed physical unit for these cells.

table.name: MBT Flame Speed Map
table.description: Supplies the modeled combustion/flame-speed term used to calculate MBT, the timing for best torque. Read it by engine speed and cylinder filling. The displayed cc/ms values describe the model term, not spark advance or measured flame travel speed. Changing this term changes the underlying timing calculation; it is not a one-for-one timing trim.

table.name: QH0 High Flow Quantity Table
table.description: High-range curve in the throttle-related airflow model. QH0 is the ECU model quantity shown on the axis of several fuel-compensation maps. Values are normalized flow potential, displayed as a percentage of the model scale; larger values assign a larger model quantity to the same input. The horizontal axis is the modeled throttle-opening-area/speed input shown in the editor. This is not throttle command percentage or a MAF voltage-to-flow curve.

table.name: QH0 Low Flow Quantity Table
table.description: Low-range curve in the throttle-related airflow model. QH0 is the ECU model quantity shown on the axis of several fuel-compensation maps. Values are normalized flow potential, displayed as a percentage of the model scale; larger values assign a larger model quantity to the same input. The horizontal axis is the modeled throttle-opening-area/speed input shown in the editor. This is not throttle command percentage or a MAF voltage-to-flow curve.

table.name: Coolant Temperature MBT Compensation Table
table.description: First coolant-temperature factor in the MBT timing model. MBT means the timing calculated for best torque. Read the curve at coolant temperature; temperatures are displayed in Fahrenheit. Values are percentage-form factors used inside the calculation, not degrees to add. Final timing depends on the other model terms, so increasing a cell is not labelled as a guaranteed increase in advance.

table.name: Coolant Temperature MBT Compensation Table 2
table.description: Second coolant-temperature factor in the MBT timing model. Read it at coolant temperature in Fahrenheit. The percentage is a calculation factor rather than degrees of advance; this table works with the other MBT factors. Its number alone does not tell you the final spark angle or a guaranteed direction of timing change.

table.name: Target AFR MBT Compensation Table 2
table.description: Second mixture-related factor in the MBT timing calculation. MBT means the timing calculated to produce best torque. The axis is target lambda: 1.0 is stoichiometric, below 1.0 is richer, and above 1.0 is leaner. Values are a percentage-form factor used with other parts of the calculation. This is not an AFR target or a direct timing addition; increasing it does not have a verified simple relationship to final advance.

table.name: Cold Idle Ignition Timing Table
table.description: Base ignition angle for the cold-idle schedule, read by engine RPM. Values are signed degrees in the idle timing calculation; a larger value advances this base schedule and a smaller value retards it. Temperature additions and other idle corrections can change final timing. This table changes timing at idle, not the target idle speed; complete schedule-selection conditions are not described by this curve alone.

table.name: Idle Ignition Timing Table
table.description: Base ignition angle for the alternate idle schedule, read by engine RPM. Values are signed degrees in the idle timing calculation; a larger value advances this base schedule and a smaller value retards it. Temperature additions and other idle corrections can change final timing. This table changes timing at idle, not the target idle speed; complete schedule-selection conditions are not described by this curve alone.

table.name: Drive Idle Ignition Timing Addition Table
table.description: Adds timing to the idle schedule in the in-gear state, according to coolant temperature. Values are degrees of advance added: 0 adds nothing and 5 adds 5 degrees before the final limit. Increasing a value increases this addition. The axis is Fahrenheit; the result works with the base idle timing schedule rather than setting idle RPM.

table.name: Neutral Idle Ignition Timing Addition Table
table.description: Adds timing to the idle schedule in the neutral state, according to coolant temperature. Values are degrees of advance added: 0 adds nothing and 5 adds 5 degrees before the final limit. Increasing a value increases this addition. The axis is Fahrenheit; the result works with the base idle timing schedule rather than setting idle RPM.

table.name: Startup ISC Airflow Initial Value
table.description: Sets the temperature-dependent starting quantity for the extra startup idle-air contribution. ISC means idle-speed control. Larger values produce a larger starting contribution when the ramp and RPM multiplier are unchanged. Values are internal air-control counts, not airflow in g/s or a target RPM. The contribution is reduced by the startup decay control.

table.name: Startup ISC Airflow Decay Value
table.description: How much the startup idle-air ramp is reduced at each eligible decay step after cranking. The interval is estimated at 512 ms (100 main control updates). Larger positive values remove the startup contribution faster; smaller values retain it longer. The ramp starts at 255 and stops at zero. Constant decay 5 requires 51 eligible steps, approximately 26.1 seconds of nominal step intervals; decay 85 requires 3, approximately 1.54 seconds. The first eligible step depends on timer phase, and changing coolant temperature can change the selected decay value. These examples are not guaranteed startup durations. The separate Base Quantity contribution decreases on the faster main schedule. Time estimate assumes a 10 MHz crystal, the documented x4 CPU clock multiplier, a 20 MHz peripheral clock and PSCR1 = 0. The crystal marking, exact MCU variant and live prescaler are unconfirmed. PSCR1 = 1 would double the interval. Operating gates and delayed processing can skip or combine eligible events. The displayed value remains the amount per step, not an amount per second.

table.name: Startup ISC Airflow Base Quantity
table.description: Sets the base startup idle-air quantity for each coolant temperature. Higher values start with a larger base quantity before later processing. Units are internal idle-air control counts, not valve opening percentage or target RPM. After cranking, this contribution decreases on every main update, estimated every 5.12 ms assuming a 10 MHz crystal, x4 CPU clock, 20 MHz peripheral clock and PSCR1 = 0. Those assumptions are unconfirmed; PSCR1 = 1 doubles the interval and delayed processing can combine updates. This is a stored starting quantity, so its unit remains counts. It is separate from the Initial Value contribution and Decay Value ramp; the latter has an estimated 512 ms step interval. Changing the ramp-decay table does not change this separate base-quantity decrease.

table.name: Ignition Timing Main Constant
table.description: A model constant used to calculate the combustion-duration portion of base ignition timing. Its displayed grams relate to the model mass term; the value is not a direct timing angle or a measured cylinder air mass. Increasing it increases that mass-related term before the other model operations. Use the ignition adjustment maps for an explicit degree-based timing change; the constant does not have a simple degrees-per-unit effect.

table.name: Ignition Delay Time
table.description: Delay term added to the calculated combustion duration before it is converted into an engine-speed-dependent timing angle. Values are milliseconds. A larger value adds more modeled delay; the resulting angle depends on RPM and the rest of the timing calculation. This is not a direct number of degrees to retard ignition.

table.name: Acceleration Fuel Compensation Map
table.description: Supplies a fresh-air compensation/model factor used during acceleration. Read it by QH0 flow quantity and engine speed. Values are displayed as percentages of the model quantity, not target AFR or a direct percentage added to injector duration. Increasing the factor does not have a fully established one-for-one effect on delivered fuel.

table.name: Deceleration Fuel Compensation Map
table.description: Supplies a fresh-air compensation/model factor used during deceleration. Read it by QH0 flow quantity and engine speed. Values are percentage-form model quantities, not the RPM threshold for fuel cut or a direct AFR target. The downstream fuel calculation determines the final effect; the cell value alone is not a stated percentage change in injector duration.

table.name: Fuel Compensation Map (16x16)
table.description: Supplies the main dimensionless fuel-compensation factor, indexed by QH0 flow quantity and engine speed. Percent display expresses the factor: 100% is 1.0, 110% is 1.1, and 90% is 0.9. This is a compensation input to the fuel calculation, not an AFR target. Other fuel corrections and limits still determine the final injector pulse.

table.name: Cylinder Fresh Air Rate Map
table.description: Models the fresh-air fraction/compensation for each engine-speed and cylinder-filling point. Values are displayed as percentages of the modeled quantity. This table supports the air and fuel model; it is not a direct target AFR, injector duty cycle or throttle-opening percentage. A simple percentage-to-final-fuel tuning rule has not been established.

table.name: Load Base Fuel Schedule Table
table.description: Reference pulse-duration curve used to calculate operating load. Select the value at engine RPM; the reference is displayed in milliseconds. Although it uses pulse-duration units, it is not a command to hold the injector open for that time. Changing it changes the load reference used by other calculations, so its effect cannot be treated as a direct fuel addition.

table.name: High Coolant Temperature Increase Compensation Table
table.description: Coolant-temperature factor for the high-temperature fuel-increase calculation. Read it from 176 to 239 degrees Fahrenheit. It is multiplied by the selected High Temperature Fuel Compensation Map value before later limits and smoothing. A zero from either table makes their product zero; 100% here means a factor of 1.0, not 100% extra fuel. Both ROMs have zeros throughout this coolant curve in stock form.

table.name: High Temperature Fuel Compensation Map
table.description: Sets the speed/load factor in the high-temperature fuel-increase calculation. Columns are cylinder-filling ranges and rows are engine-speed ranges, numbered 0 through 3. Their boundaries are editable in the two High Temperature Fuel Bin Upper Limits tables. The ECU picks one cell without blending neighboring cells. This factor is multiplied by the coolant-temperature factor; a zero from either table makes the product zero. A cell is not by itself a direct percentage of extra injector pulse.

table.name: High Temperature Fuel RPM Bin Upper Limits
table.description: Defines the three RPM boundaries between the four rows of High Temperature Fuel Compensation Map. With stock values, row 0 is at or below 2000 RPM, row 1 is above 2000 through 3600, row 2 is above 3600 through 12700, and row 3 is above 12700. Equality stays in the lower row. The high final boundary leaves the last row unused at ordinary engine speeds; it is not a rev limit. Editing a boundary moves the division between rows. Keep the values ascending.

table.name: High Temperature Fuel Filling Bin Upper Limits
table.description: Defines the three cylinder-filling boundaries between the four columns of High Temperature Fuel Compensation Map. Stock divisions are 20.3125%, 39.84375% and 48.4375% filling. Column 0 is at or below the first boundary; each higher column starts only above the next boundary, with column 3 above the last. These percentages describe cylinder filling, not throttle opening. Editing a boundary moves the division between columns. Keep the values ascending.

table.name: Individual Cylinder Fuel Trims
table.description: Scales the calculated fuel quantity for each cylinder. 100% leaves that cylinder quantity unchanged, 110% increases it by 10%, and 90% decreases it by 10%, before any later processing. This balances cylinder quantities; it does not change the main AFR target. The four entries are the ECU cylinder indices shown on the axis.

table.name: Target AFR Map (8x8)
table.description: Sets the mixture target by engine speed and cylinder filling. Values use the gasoline AFR scale: lower AFR is richer and higher AFR is leaner; 14.7 corresponds to lambda 1.0 on this scale. For example, 12.5 is richer than 14.7. This is a commanded target rather than a measured AFR, and other compensation or operating modes can change it. The gasoline display scale is retained even when interpreting other fuels.

table.name: Target AFR Compensation Multiplier (High Detonation)
table.description: Scales how far the main mixture target is from stoichiometric when this compensation is selected. 100% leaves that deviation unchanged. Above 100% moves it farther from stoichiometric; below 100% brings it closer. Thus a rich main target becomes richer with a larger factor, while a lean main target becomes leaner. This does not multiply the displayed AFR number directly. Read the curve by RPM. Stock values are 100%; the complete operating-state conditions selecting this curve remain under investigation.

table.name: Closed Loop to Open Loop Delay
table.description: Maximum transition-delay threshold for the identified stage of the closed-loop/open-loop fuel state machine. A larger value permits a longer delay at this stage. The ECU stores a byte threshold, stock 26, and compares it with the high byte of an internal timer. The current seconds display uses a reference conversion of 0.2 seconds per threshold count; stock therefore displays 5.2 reference seconds. That conversion came from the reference calibration, and actual elapsed seconds have not been confirmed for this ECU clock and timer. Treat the display as provisional rather than an exact wait after a throttle change. Other stages and operating conditions also apply.

table.name: K-Value
table.description: Main conversion constant linking calculated air quantity to injector pulse duration. Increasing it increases the calculated fuel term when its other inputs are unchanged; decreasing it reduces that term. The displayed ms/kg is a conversion constant, not injector size in cc/min. It works with MAF Factor, the MAF curve, injector latency and later fuel corrections.

table.name: MAF Factor
table.description: Factory air-quantity unit factor used with K-Value in the main fuel calculation. Increasing it increases that calculated fuel term when the other inputs are unchanged. The displayed kg/hr scale describes the factor conversion; it is not a measured airflow reading or a maximum sensor-flow limit. It does not replace the voltage-to-flow shape of MAF Table.

table.name: Minimum Injector Pulse Width
table.description: Lower limit on the calculated base injector pulse, in milliseconds. If that base calculation is below the limit, the ECU raises it to this value. A higher value raises the minimum base fuel quantity. Latency, cylinder corrections and trims are applied afterward, so this is not necessarily the shortest final electrical pulse measured at an injector.

table.name: Maximum Injector Pulsewidth Table
table.description: Upper limit used to clamp the calculated main fuel quantity at each engine speed, displayed in milliseconds. Increasing a value allows a larger pulse quantity at that RPM; it does not command the injector to stay open that long. This limit is part of the fuel calculation and does not by itself specify injector duty cycle or flow capacity.

table.name: Rev Limit Fuel Cut Mode A
table.description: Engine speed at which rev-limit mode A requests fuel cut. Values are RPM; increasing the value raises this cut threshold. Use the matching Fuel Restore value to define when fuel can resume as speed falls. Mode A and B are separate state selections; their complete selection conditions remain unresolved.

table.name: Rev Limit Fuel Cut Mode B
table.description: Engine speed at which rev-limit mode B requests fuel cut. Values are RPM; increasing the value raises this cut threshold. Use the matching Fuel Restore value to define when fuel can resume as speed falls. Mode A and B are separate state selections; their complete selection conditions remain unresolved.

table.name: Rev Limit Fuel Restore Mode A
table.description: Engine-speed threshold for restoring fuel as RPM falls in rev-limit mode A. The separation from the matching Fuel Cut threshold provides the cut/restore gap. A higher restore value permits fuel to resume at a higher RPM. Keep it below the matching cut value to retain that gap. This is not a second fuel-cut threshold; the complete conditions selecting mode A remain unresolved.

table.name: Rev Limit Fuel Restore Mode B
table.description: Engine-speed threshold for restoring fuel as RPM falls in rev-limit mode B. The separation from the matching Fuel Cut threshold provides the cut/restore gap. A higher restore value permits fuel to resume at a higher RPM. Keep it below the matching cut value to retain that gap. This is not a second fuel-cut threshold; the complete conditions selecting mode B remain unresolved.

table.name: Bosch Fuel Cut Table
table.description: Coolant-temperature-based RPM threshold for engaging deceleration fuel cut in the Bosch airflow configuration. Read the axis in Fahrenheit and the cells in RPM. A higher value raises the speed required for this cut threshold. It works with the matching Restore table and the other deceleration conditions. This is separate from the high-RPM rev limiter; a table being present does not establish that its configuration is active on this vehicle.

table.name: JECS Fuel Cut Table
table.description: Coolant-temperature-based RPM threshold for engaging deceleration fuel cut in the JECS airflow configuration. Read the axis in Fahrenheit and the cells in RPM. A higher value raises the speed required for this cut threshold. It works with the matching Restore table and the other deceleration conditions. This is separate from the high-RPM rev limiter; a table being present does not establish that its configuration is active on this vehicle.

table.name: Bosch Fuel Restore Table
table.description: Coolant-temperature-based RPM threshold for restoring fuel as speed falls during deceleration in the Bosch airflow configuration. Read the axis in Fahrenheit and the cells in RPM. A higher value permits fuel to resume at a higher RPM. It works with the matching Cut table and the other deceleration conditions. This is separate from the high-RPM rev limiter; a table being present does not establish that its configuration is active on this vehicle.

table.name: JECS Fuel Restore Table
table.description: Coolant-temperature-based RPM threshold for restoring fuel as speed falls during deceleration in the JECS airflow configuration. Read the axis in Fahrenheit and the cells in RPM. A higher value permits fuel to resume at a higher RPM. It works with the matching Cut table and the other deceleration conditions. This is separate from the high-RPM rev limiter; a table being present does not establish that its configuration is active on this vehicle.

table.name: Target Idle RPM Table
table.description: Sets the idle-speed target for each coolant temperature, displayed in RPM. Increasing a value asks the idle controller to hold a higher speed at that temperature. The ECU uses air and timing adjustments to approach the target; the number is not a rev limiter and does not guarantee the measured idle under every load. Temperatures on the axis are Fahrenheit.

table.name: Lean Burn Idle Ignition Timing Table
table.description: Base ignition angle for the lean-burn idle schedule, read by engine RPM. Values are signed degrees in the idle timing calculation; a larger value advances this base schedule and a smaller value retards it. Temperature additions and other idle corrections can change final timing. This table changes timing at idle, not the target idle speed; complete schedule-selection conditions are not described by this curve alone.

table.name: Initial Retard Quantity Table (Fuel Cut)
table.description: Initial amount of ignition retard used during the fuel-cut transition, displayed as positive degrees to remove. A larger value requests a larger initial retard amount; it is not the final spark angle. The axis describes the change in throttle opening over 10 milliseconds rather than absolute throttle position. Later transition processing still applies.

table.name: MAF Offset
table.description: Offset subtracted in the MAF conversion, shown in native ECU counts. For an otherwise unchanged conversion input, a larger offset makes the value after subtraction smaller. Counts are not volts or g/s. This works with the MAF transfer curve and unit factors; the complete final-fuel effect is not a one-count-to-one-unit airflow change.

table.name: MAF Table
table.description: Converts mass-airflow sensor voltage into the ECU airflow-conversion quantity. Read the horizontal axis in volts; the cells remain native ECU transfer counts, not directly g/s. A larger cell assigns a larger conversion quantity to that voltage before offsets, unit factors and later calculations. This curve describes sensor response; the separate MAF voltage thresholds control fault checks.

table.name: MAF Stable-Signal Voltage Lower Limit
table.description: Lower edge of the voltage band in which the P0100 stable-signal test can qualify. A signal must be at or above this value, below the upper limit, and have sufficiently small voltage variation, with the required operating conditions and delay. Lowering this edge widens that test band; raising it narrows the band. This is not the basic low-voltage fault threshold or the MAF flow limit.

table.name: MAF Stable-Signal Voltage Upper Limit
table.description: Upper edge of the voltage band in which the P0100 stable-signal test can qualify. A signal must be below this value, at or above the lower limit, and have sufficiently small voltage variation, with the required operating conditions and delay. Raising this edge widens that test band; lowering it narrows the band. This is not the basic high-voltage fault threshold or the MAF flow limit.

table.name: MAF Voltage Upper Limit
table.description: Voltage threshold for the basic high-signal P0100 fault check. A signal at or above this value can qualify, subject to operating conditions and a fault delay. Raising it permits a higher voltage before this check qualifies; lowering it makes the check qualify at a lower voltage. A separate control routine also uses this threshold, so it is not exclusively a diagnostic setting. Other plausibility tests have their own thresholds.

table.name: MAF Voltage Lower Limit
table.description: Voltage threshold for the basic low-signal P0100 fault check. A signal below this value can qualify, subject to operating conditions and a fault delay. Lowering it permits a lower voltage before this check qualifies; raising it makes the check qualify at a higher voltage. A separate control routine also uses this threshold. The stable-signal and RPM/throttle plausibility tests remain separate.

table.name: P0340 Reporting (Record 0)
table.description: Controls whether this P0340 record appears in the verified standard stored-code responses. 0 allows reporting; 1 suppresses this record from the Mode 03 stored-code list and Mode 01 PID 01 fault-count/MIL-status response. This changes reporting, not the fault test itself. It is not a verified physical check-engine-lamp switch. Pending-code and manufacturer-specific responses can still expose the fault. Repeated codes have separate records; this switch affects only the named record. Other record bits are preserved.

table.name: Knock Timing Recovery Step
table.description: How much removed timing is restored on each eligible recovery step, estimated every 51.2 ms (10 main control updates). Recovery also requires no accumulated knock-detection count and active recovery conditions. Stock +0.1016 degrees moves a -3.0000 degree correction to about -2.8984 before other processing. Continuous eligible stock recovery would average about 1.98 degrees/second. Larger positive values restore timing in larger steps. The Maximum Change control runs on the faster main-update schedule. Time estimate assumes a 10 MHz crystal, the documented x4 CPU clock multiplier, a 20 MHz peripheral clock and PSCR1 = 0. The crystal marking, exact MCU variant and live prescaler are unconfirmed. PSCR1 = 1 would double the interval. Operating gates and delayed processing can skip or combine eligible events. The displayed value remains the amount per step, not an amount per second.

table.name: Knock Timing Retard per Count
table.description: How much timing the count-based correction requests to remove for each accumulated knock-detection count. Stock is about 1.1992 degrees per count, so two counts request about 2.3984 degrees of additional retard before limits. The main timing calculation reads and clears accumulated counts each main update, estimated every 5.12 ms assuming a 10 MHz crystal, x4 CPU clock, 20 MHz peripheral clock and PSCR1 = 0. Those clock assumptions are unconfirmed; PSCR1 = 1 doubles the interval and delayed processing can combine pending updates. Counts are produced by completed engine-related knock sampling windows, not at a fixed count rate and not necessarily one per knocking combustion event. The unit remains degrees/count. Larger positive values request more retard per count. Maximum Change and total-retard limits can reduce the actual change.

table.name: Knock Sensor Failure Timing Correction
table.description: Signed timing-correction value selected when the knock-sensor failure status is active. Stock -5 degrees proposes removal of 5 degrees; zero proposes no offset, and positive values propose advance. More-negative values propose more retard. Subsequent correction processing still applies, so the value does not guarantee that final ignition timing is exactly 5 degrees lower. Sensor-fault diagnosis and code reporting are separate controls.

table.name: Knock Timing Correction Maximum Change
table.description: Limits how far the accumulated knock correction can move from its previous value on each normal main control update, in either direction. The update interval is estimated at 5.12 ms. Stock 5 degrees allows up to a 5-degree change per update: a move from -2 to -8 degrees is limited to -7 before the total-retard limit is applied. Larger values permit bigger changes without increasing the total allowed retard. Recovery is eligible only once every 10 main updates. This is a per-update limit, not a guaranteed rate of timing change. The octane-schedule transition uses separate processing. Time estimate assumes a 10 MHz crystal, the documented x4 CPU clock multiplier, a 20 MHz peripheral clock and PSCR1 = 0. The crystal marking, exact MCU variant and live prescaler are unconfirmed. PSCR1 = 1 would double the interval. Operating gates and delayed processing can skip or combine eligible events. The displayed value remains the amount per step, not an amount per second.

table.name: High Octane Knock Retard Limit Map
table.description: Maximum amount of timing the normal knock-correction path is allowed to remove in the high-octane state. Cells are positive retard amounts: 10 permits a correction down to -10 degrees; it does not immediately command 10 degrees of retard. A larger value allows more total retard, while a smaller value restricts it. Zero prevents negative accumulated correction in this normal path; it does not switch off knock detection or every protection path. Columns are engine-speed ranges and rows are ECU-load ranges. Use Knock Retard Speed Bin Upper Limits and Knock Retard Load Bin Upper Limits for their current boundaries. Stock speed ranges are <=2400, >2400 through 4800, and >4800 RPM; stock load ranges are <=41, >41 through 76, and >76 ECU counts. The ECU selects one cell without blending. Sensor-failure and schedule-transition processing can follow different conditions.

table.name: High Detonation Knock Retard Limit Map
table.description: Maximum amount of timing the normal knock-correction path is allowed to remove in the alternate detonation-protection fuel state. The name describes the selected operating state, not a knock-strength axis. Cells are positive retard amounts: 10 permits a correction down to -10 degrees; it does not immediately command 10 degrees of retard. A larger value allows more total retard, while a smaller value restricts it. Zero prevents negative accumulated correction in this normal path; it does not switch off knock detection or every protection path. Columns are engine-speed ranges and rows are ECU-load ranges. Use Knock Retard Speed Bin Upper Limits and Knock Retard Load Bin Upper Limits for their current boundaries. Stock speed ranges are <=2400, >2400 through 4800, and >4800 RPM; stock load ranges are <=41, >41 through 76, and >76 ECU counts. The ECU selects one cell without blending. Sensor-failure and schedule-transition processing can follow different conditions.

table.name: Knock Retard Speed Bin Upper Limits
table.description: Defines the boundaries between the three columns of both Knock Retard Limit maps. With stock values: Low is at or below 2400 RPM; Middle is above 2400 through 4800 RPM; High is above 4800 RPM. Equality stays in the lower range. Increasing a boundary extends the lower range to a higher RPM. Map labels identify ranges and follow the current boundary values; they are not fixed RPM points. Keep the boundaries ascending.

table.name: Knock Retard Load Bin Upper Limits
table.description: Defines the boundaries between the three rows of both Knock Retard Limit maps. With stock values: Low is at or below 41 ECU load counts; Middle is above 41 through 76; High is above 76. Equality stays in the lower range. Increasing a boundary extends the lower range to a higher load-count value. Counts are the internal ECU load signal; they have not been converted to filling percentage or airflow. Keep the boundaries ascending.

table.name: Knock Slice Map
table.description: Detection threshold for the processed knock signal after background correction, for each cylinder slot and engine speed. A signal strictly above the threshold produces a detection count. Raising a cell requires a stronger processed signal and makes detection less sensitive; lowering it makes detection more sensitive. Units are a normalized knock index, not sensor volts, a percentage or retard degrees. The ECU blends between RPM points and uses the nearest end value outside 400-6400 RPM. Slots 1-4 are firmware slots; their physical cylinder/firing-order mapping is not confirmed.

table.name: Knock Sensor Diagnosis Voltage Lower Limit
table.description: Lowest nominal circuit voltage that passes the P0325 knock-sensor range check. Stock 1.00 V is accepted at this lower edge; the signal must also be below the upper limit, stock 4.00 V. Lowering this value widens the accepted voltage range; raising it narrows the range. Operating conditions and a fault delay also apply. This checks the sensor circuit, not combustion-knock strength, and does not set how much timing is removed.

table.name: Knock Sensor Diagnosis Voltage Upper Limit
table.description: Upper nominal circuit-voltage boundary for the P0325 knock-sensor range check. The signal must be below this value: stock 4.00 V itself is outside the accepted range. It must also be at or above the lower limit, stock 1.00 V. Raising this value widens the accepted range; lowering it narrows it. Operating conditions and a fault delay also apply. This checks the sensor circuit rather than combustion-knock sensitivity or timing retard.
